top_cluster.headline: Sherrod Brown is running for his old Ohio Senate seat in a race widely seen as pivotal to which party controls the Senate, with his appeal to working-class voters seen as the deciding factor.
top_cluster.left_framing: Washington Post elevates the race to national stakes, presenting it as a bellwether that could determine Senate control, and centers the narrative on Brown needing to win back working-class voters who defected to Trump.
top_cluster.center_framing: RealClearPolitics treats the race as an open, uncertain question about Brown's personal political viability — whether his working-class brand still resonates — without framing it in terms of broader Senate power dynamics.
top_cluster.right_framing: No right-leaning source is included in this set; only left and center-right outlets are represented.
top_cluster.left_omissions: The Washington Post's framing does not surface the more skeptical, comeback-in-doubt tone found in center-right coverage, which questions whether Brown's appeal still works rather than assuming it's simply a swing-state proxy battle.
top_cluster.right_omissions: No right-leaning outlet is present in this coverage set, so it's not possible to assess what a right-leaning framing omits relative to the left.

blindspot_narrative: Right-leaning outlets are systematically avoiding or minimizing stories where GOP-aligned actors or agencies are the subject of accountability (Massie's impeachment filing, the ICE First Amendment loss), while left-leaning outlets are absent from stories that would require engaging with intra-Democrat coalition or oversight-overreach critiques (the Hill's warning about Democratic oversight tools backfiring). Both sides are ignoring the same underlying thread — a bipartisan-flavored skepticism of expansive executive/agency power — because acknowledging it cuts against each side's preferred story of the other party as uniquely authoritarian.
